title: Defect control in metamaterial self-assembly
bottleneck: Self-assembly via block copolymers or colloidal crystallization can pattern nanostructures over large areas cheaply, but defect densities are orders of magnitude above what functional metamaterials tolerate: grain boundaries, dislocations, and missing features scatter waves and destroy the designed response. Directed self-assembly with templating helps locally but reintroduces the cost and throughput limits it was meant to escape.
why_it_blocks: Self-assembly is the only plausible route to metamaterials at commodity scale and cost. Uncontrolled defects mean the optical, acoustic, or mechanical performance never matches design, so products built on self-assembled metamaterials cannot be specified or warranted.
current_state: Hierarchical assembly and error-correcting designs that tolerate defects are active research areas, with improving but still inadequate order over large areas. The field lacks a quantitative defect budget linking assembly statistics to device yield.
